summary: Almost every visitor to Cuba needs a tourist card — the tarjeta del turista, now issued electronically — valid for a 30-day stay (90 days for Canadians) and extendable once, plus mandatory travel medical insurance and the online D'Viajeros declaration. Only a short list of countries, mostly Russia, China and Cuba's Caribbean neighbors, is exempt.

AF.notes: A tourist card (tarjeta del turista) is required — now issued electronically. Buy it online, from a Cuban consulate or through your airline, then complete the D'Viajeros declaration and carry proof of medical insurance valid in Cuba. If the online system does not accept your nationality, apply through a Cuban consulate.

passportValidity.text: Travel with a passport valid for at least six months on arrival. Cuba's formal rule is validity for the period of stay, but airlines and consulates apply the six-month standard when issuing tourist cards.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba
MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required from travelers aged one year and over arriving from — or having recently transited — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. No vaccination is required if you fly in directly from Europe, North America or the rest of the Caribbean.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

travelInsurance.text: Travel medical insurance valid in Cuba is a legal condition of entry and officers can ask for proof. Policies issued by US insurers are generally not accepted; travelers without recognized cover must buy a Cuban policy at the airport before clearing immigration.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

onwardTicket.text: A confirmed return or onward ticket is required, together with proof of accommodation — a hotel booking or the address and details of the casa particular you are staying in.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

proofOfFunds.text: No published minimum, but Cuba is largely a cash economy for visitors — bring enough euros, Canadian dollars, pounds or US dollars in cash to cover the whole trip.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

declarations.name: D'Viajeros traveler information form
declarations.text: Every traveler must complete the free D'Viajeros online form — a combined immigration, customs and health declaration — within 72 hours before arrival, and present the QR code at the airport. It is separate from the tourist card and does not replace it.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

currencyLimits.text: Amounts of USD 5,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared on arrival. Taking Cuban pesos out of the country is prohibited, and unspent pesos are difficult to change back.

source.name: MINREX — Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Cuba

notes: Drones are prohibited — they are confiscated on arrival and returned, at best, on departure.
Satellite phones, GPS trackers and professional broadcast equipment require prior authorization.
Medicines are scarce locally: bring what you need in original packaging, with a prescription for anything unusual. Donated medicines and toiletries are welcomed but should be declared.

payments.text: Cuba runs on cash for visitors. Cards issued by US banks do not work at all, and other foreign cards are unreliable — bring euros, Canadian dollars, pounds or US dollars in cash and change what you need. Some hotels and state shops take payment only by card in foreign currency, so carry both if you can.

safety.text: Violent crime against tourists is rare, but pickpocketing and scams around Havana's tourist areas are common. The bigger practical risks are long power cuts, fuel and medicine shortages and thin emergency services outside the main cities.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Cuba Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is dry and warm — the best months for Havana and the beaches. The hurricane season runs from June to November, and September and October are the wettest.

idp.text: Cuba is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Cuba is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Cuba yet.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

tips.text: Bring all the money you will need in cash. Cards issued by US banks never work in Cuba, other foreign cards frequently fail, and ATMs are unreliable — euros and Canadian dollars are the easiest currencies to change.

Visiting Cuba costs you the US visa waiver: anyone who has traveled to Cuba since January 12, 2021 is ineligible for ESTA and must apply for a US visa instead. Plan any US trip around that before you book.

US citizens may travel to Cuba only under one of the OFAC general license categories — "support for the Cuban people" is the usual one; pure tourism is not permitted. Keep records of your itinerary and spending for five years.
Fill in the D'Viajeros form within 72 hours of arrival and screenshot the QR code — mobile data at Havana airport is patchy and the code is checked before immigration.
Carry a printed insurance certificate showing medical coverage valid in Cuba. Without one you will be sent to buy a Cuban policy at the airport counter before you can enter.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Cuba?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes — but it is a tourist card (tarjeta del turista) rather than a full visa, and it is now issued electronically. It allows a 30-day stay (90 days for Canadians), extendable once for the same period. Only a short list of countries — including Russia, China, Belarus, Serbia and several Caribbean neighbors — is exempt.

faq.question: Can US citizens travel to Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes, but not as ordinary tourists. US law requires travel to fall under one of the OFAC general license categories, most commonly "support for the Cuban people". You still need the tourist card, cannot use US-issued bank cards in Cuba, and must keep records of the trip for five years.

faq.question: Does visiting Cuba affect US ESTA?
faq.answer: Yes. Anyone who has visited Cuba on or after January 12, 2021 is no longer eligible to enter the United States under the Visa Waiver Program and must obtain a US visa instead. This applies to all nationalities, not just US-bound Europeans, so consider the order of your trips carefully.

faq.question: Is travel insurance mandatory for Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes. Medical insurance valid in Cuba is a legal entry requirement and can be checked at the border. Policies from US insurers are generally not accepted — if you cannot show recognized cover, you must buy a Cuban policy at the airport.

faq.question: What is the D'Viajeros form?
faq.answer: It is Cuba's free online arrival declaration, covering immigration, customs and health information. Complete it at dviajeros.mitrans.gob.cu within 72 hours before you arrive and show the QR code at the airport. It is required in addition to the tourist card.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes. A tourist card can normally be extended once, by another 30 days (90 for Canadians), at an immigration office before it expires. Overstaying causes problems on departure, so apply a few days early — your accommodation host can usually point you to the right office.
